brave.title: Confined Spaces: Is 19.5 Percent Oxygen Really Safe? | EHS Today
brave.snippet:
Some gases and vapors may be present at concentrations well above the TLV while, at the same time, they are below a combustible gas meter's limit of detection. Because ambient air contains about 20.8 percent oxygen, if the oxygen concentration in a space is anything other than 20.8 percent, you should ask yourself "Why?". If you can't come up with a credible answer, you had better not let people enter a space until you can do so. John Rekus is an independent safety consultant and author of the National Safety Council's Complete Confined Spaces Handbook.
Everybody knows that an oxygen level of 19.5 percent is safe for entry into confined spaces. Well, once again, what everybody knows is simply wrong!
For example, in the first case I worked on as an expert witness, the entry supervisor for a contract tank cleaning firm tested the atmosphere in a space and found it contained 20.1 percent oxygen. When I saw that number, I was concerned, very concerned. The supervisor wasn't; in fact, he was oblivious to the warning it provided. Instead, he testified with great confidence that he knew that 19.5 percent was "safe." After all, that's what he'd been taught at the confined space course he took at the state fire school.
The oxygen partial pressure inside a confined space may be lower than the 159 mm Hg found in ambient air. If so, the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolar spaces also will be lower. If inert gases like argon and nitrogen enter a space, they displace some of the atmospheric air. When this happens, the amount of oxygen and, thus, its partial pressure goes down. For example, assume that nitrogen leaks into a space, lowering the oxygen level to 19.5 percent.

brave.title: Minimum Oxygen Levels in Confined Spaces: Safety Thresholds and Best Practices – Bridge Legal
brave.snippet:
Regulatory guidance in the United States centers on establishing a safe lower limit for entry. The generally accepted minimum acceptable oxygen level for confined-space entry is 19.5 percent by volume. Readings below 19.5 percent are considered oxygen-deficient and pose serious risks of asphyxiation.
The key takeaway is to maintain atmospheric oxygen within the 19.5 percent to 23.5 percent range to minimize both suffocation and fire risks. Beyond oxygen content, employers must assess other atmospheric hazards, such as lower explosive limits (LEL) for combustible gases, hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, and other toxic air contaminants. OSHA standards for permit-required confined spaces require atmospheric testing before and during entry, with continuous monitoring for long-duration tasks or changing conditions.
While the 19.5 percent minimum is widely recognized, site-specific risk assessments may adjust practices to remain within safe operation bands. Accurate measurement of oxygen concentration relies on calibrated detectors designed for confined-space work. The most common instruments are electrochemical oxygen sensors and paramagnetic or ultrasonic oxygen analyzers.
In summary, the minimum acceptable oxygen level for confined-space entry is 19.5 percent by volume, with a recommended safe operating range up to 23.5 percent to minimize fire risk.

brave-llmcontext.title: Confined Spaces: Is 19.5 Percent Oxygen Really Safe?
brave-llmcontext.snippet:
Note the subtle difference here. The standard does not say that atmospheres containing 19.5 percent are safe; it says that those which have levels below 19.5 percent *may be hazardous*. While this might sound like hairsplitting, I"ll explain later why it isn't.
Normal atmospheric air at sea level has a pressure of 760 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). Because air contains approximately 21 percent oxygen, oxygen's contribution to the total pressure, in other words its partial pressure, is 21 percent of 760 mm Hg, or about 159 mm Hg. But as fresh air enters the upper respiratory tract, it is humidified and the water vapor lowers the partial pressure of oxygen to about 150 mm Hg.
If inert gases like argon and nitrogen enter a space, they displace some of the atmospheric air. When this happens, the amount of oxygen and, thus, its partial pressure goes down. For example, assume that nitrogen leaks into a space, lowering the oxygen level to 19.5 percent. The oxygen partial pressure is now 19.5 percent of 760 mm Hg, or 148 mm Hg.
Contrary to popular belief, 19.5 percent oxygen is not some magic number.  Some gases and vapors may be present at concentrations well above the TLV while, at the same time, they are below a combustible gas meter's limit of detection.

Regulatory guidance in the United States centers on establishing a safe lower limit for entry. Readings below 19.5 percent are considered oxygen-deficient and pose serious risks of asphyxiation. Workers may not notice the danger until symptoms become severe, underscoring the need for reliable monitoring and strict adherence to entry procedures.

Confined Space Hazards

57. What is oxygen deficiency?  
Air normally contains 21 percent oxygen. Oxygen deficiency is created when the oxygen level falls below 19.5 percent at sea level.

58. How do oxygen-deficient environments develop?  
Oxygen deficiency can be caused by:  
• Combustion (fire, welding, and operation of internal combustion engines all consume oxygen).  
• Formation of rust (consumes oxygen).  
• Decomposition of organic matter (consumes oxygen and produces flammable methane gas, which can also displace oxygen).  
• Displacement by a heavy gas that has settled in a low-lying space or by another vapor (an inert gas such as argon, carbon dioxide, or nitrogen) used to purge the space.

59. How does oxygen deficiency affect a person who enters a confined space without protection?  
Oxygen deficiency impairs judgment and breathing, often making self-rescue difficult or impossible. A severe oxygen deficiency can lead to loss of consciousness and eventual death.

Attention  
Do not enter confined spaces containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen without approved SCBA or SAR

jina.snippet:
I frequently ask participants in my confined space courses, "What makes 19.5 percent so special? Why isn't the acceptable level of oxygen something else, like 19.3 percent, 19.8 percent or 20.2 percent?" The usual answer I get is, "Because OSHA says so."

Contrary to popular belief, OSHA doesn't say that an oxygen level of 19.5 percent is "safe." Instead, 29 CFR 1910.146(b) defines a hazardous atmosphere as one "... that may expose employees to the risk of death, incapacitation, impairment, or ability to self-rescue (that is, escape unaided from a permit space), injury or acute illness from one or more of the following causes ...." The standard then goes on to list five causes, one of which is "... atmospheric oxygen concentration below 19.5 percent...."

Note the subtle difference here. The standard does not say that atmospheres containing 19.5 percent are safe; it says that those which have levels below 19.5 percent _may be hazardous_. While this might sound like hairsplitting, I"ll explain later why it isn't.

**Understanding Standards**

OSHA standards simply state regulatory requirements. They don't tell us how those requirements should be met, nor do they offer any advice, guidance, or commentary on how to achieve compliance. This is not something unique to OSHA. Codes, regulations and standards are not intended to be cookbooks that tell us how to do something; but, rather, they are documents that summarize specific expectations. **Why 19.5 percent and not something closer to 20.9?** OSHA chose 19.5 to leave a margin. The agency’s own rulemaking record says that at 16 to 19.5 percent a worker doing any kind of exertion can rapidly become symptomatic, with faster breathing, faster heartbeat and impaired thinking or coordination, and that even a momentary loss of coordination can be devastating in a confined space or at height. jina.title: OSHA Confined Space Definition: The Three Tests That Trigger Everything Else
jina.snippet:
The **OSHA confined space definition** is shorter than most people expect. Under 29 CFR 1910.146, a space qualifies if it meets three conditions at once: it is large enough for a worker to bodily enter and perform assigned work, it has limited or restricted means of entry or exit, and it is not designed for continuous occupancy.

All three must apply. A crawl space with a wide opening is not confined. A cabinet too small to enter is not confined. A tank with a manway on top meets all three, which is why tanks, vessels, pits, sewers and silos account for most of the spaces that fall under the rule.

#### Confined is not the same as permit required

The definition above establishes that a space is confined. It does not yet establish what the employer has to do about it.

A confined space becomes a permit required confined space when it also contains, or has the potential to contain, a serious hazard. A hazardous atmosphere is the most common trigger. Others include a material capable of engulfing an entrant, an internal configuration that could trap or asphyxiate, and any other recognized serious safety or health hazard.

For atmospheres, OSHA is specific about what counts as hazardous. Oxygen below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent qualifies. So does any substance present above its published permissible exposure limit, and any condition immediately dangerous to life or health.

That is the point where the definition stops being paperwork and starts requiring an instrument.

Before an employee enters, the internal atmosphere must be tested with a calibrated direct reading instrument, in a fixed order: oxygen first, then flammable gases and vapors, then potential toxic air contaminants.

linkup.title: Oxygen levels in confined spaces: what workers need to know | HSE
linkup.snippet:
When working in confined spaces, AS2865:2009 specifies both the minimum and maximum levels of oxygen in a confined space to provide a safe, respirable atmosphere for workers.  
Oxygen concentration in a confined space should not fall below 19.5 per cent and should not exceed 23.5 per cent.  
Falling below the minimum level or exceeding the maximum level can create an extremely hazardous environment for workers in that area.
The combustion of flammable materials is one of the main ways oxygen levels can be altered. Tasks like welding or cutting use oxygen when creating flames or sparks.  
When working in sewers or other similar waste systems, the bacterial reactions in organic matter can also reduce the amount of available oxygen.  
In a sufficiently small confined spaces, with poor ventilation, even the respiration (breathing) of a worker can, over time, reduce the concentration of oxygen available.

linkup.snippet:
A confined space per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 is a space large enough to enter and work in, with limited entry/exit, and not designed for continuous occupancy. Atmospheric hazards are the leading cause of confined space fatalities, including oxygen deficiency, toxic gases, and flammable atmospheres. Pre-entry atmospheric testing is mandatory.  
Oxygen must be between 19.5% and 23.5% by volume. Below 19.5% is oxygen-deficient (IDLH below 16%); above 23.5% is oxygen-enriched (fire/explosion risk). Combustible gases are measured as percent of their Lower Explosive Limit (%LEL) — action level at 10% LEL, entry prohibited above 25% LEL. Common toxic gases include H₂S (PEL 10 ppm, IDLH 100 ppm) and CO (PEL 50 ppm, IDLH 1200 ppm).  
Testing must be performed in this order: oxygen first (instruments need adequate O₂), then combustibles, then toxic gases. Monitoring must be continuous during occupancy. Testing should cover multiple levels (top, middle, bottom) as gases stratify by density — H₂S (heavier than air) sinks, methane (lighter) rises.  
Ventilation is the primary atmospheric control method. Forced-air ventilation using explosion-proof blowers should run continuously during confined space work. Air should be supplied to the lowest point (to displace heavier-than-air gases upward) at a minimum rate of 20 air changes per hour. Natural ventilation alone is rarely sufficient for permit-required confined spaces.

54-4-4: HAZARD CATEGORIES:
The most common hazards that should be recognized and associated with entry into a confined space can be categorized as follows:
A. Oxygen Deficient Or Enriched Atmospheres: Normal air contains approximately seventy eight percent (78%) nitrogen and twenty and ninety five-tenths percent (20.95%) oxygen by volume with the remaining composition made up of gases, such as argon, carbon dioxide, etc. When oxygen falls below nineteen and five-tenths percent (19.5%), asphyxiation is threatened. Likewise, when an atmosphere contains more than twenty three and five-tenths percent (23.5%) of oxygen, it can be an extremely flammable atmosphere and creates a hazard. Confined spaces with either oxygen deficient or oxygen enriched atmospheres should not be entered unless they are properly controlled, as through appropriate ventilation.
B. Flammable/Combustible Atmosphere: Two (2) situations exist which create flammable atmosphere: the availability of oxygen in the air; and a flammable gas, vapor or dust in the proper mixture. If a source of ignition is present or introduced into a confined space with the right combination of combustible gas, vapor or dust and air, an explosion will occur.
C. Toxic Atmospheres: Any chemical exhibiting toxic properties in a confined space is a cause for concern. In these cases, no entry should be made until the atmosphere is properly controlled, or the entrant is properly protected. All chemicals have a concentration at which a toxic response is elicited.

parallel-fast.title: What Is a Confined Space and Why Is It Dangerous?
parallel-fast.snippet:
Bureau of Labor Statistics.
This blog outlines the major hazards involved in confined space entry and rescue, as well as the resources NFPA ® offers to help minimize risk.

What is a confined space?

A confined space isn’t simply defined as any small space. It must be large enough to enter and perform work; have limited or restricted means for entering and exiting; and not be designed for continuous employee occupancy.
Some examples of confined spaces include crawl spaces, grain bins, manholes, and tanks of all types. Workers might need to enter these spaces to perform repairs, inspections, or maintenance, but they are not designed for somebody to work in there all day.

What hazards exist in confined spaces?

Not designed for continuous occupancy, confined spaces often have limited ventilation and other hazards that are not controlled like they would be in continuously occupied spaces. These hazards generally fall into two categories: atmospheric hazards and safety hazards.
Atmospheric hazards can include toxic contaminants, flammable vapors, and oxygen-deficient environments. More broadly, safety hazards might include mechanical hazards like rotating parts, electrical hazards like exposed wiring, fall hazards, drowning hazards, and more.

What is the leading cause of death in confined spaces?

It is generally recognized that lack of oxygen is the leading cause of death in confined spaces. For example, in 2021, three workers died in the Bahamas after entering a floating metal tank used to store scrap metal at a dock; testing later revealed that the tank had an oxygen level of just 2 percent.
Under normal conditions, the air we breathe contains approximately 21 percent oxygen. Most of the remaining 79 percent is made up of nitrogen with smaller quantities other gases such as argon and carbon dioxide.

Introduction

Part XI of the Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (COHSR) – Confined spaces has been updated. This guidance document is provided to supplement, clarify, and interpret some of its provisions.
Work performed while occupying confined spaces presents unique hazards, including:
* awkward and restricted movements
* difficulties with the provision of emergency medical support
* the atmosphere can change much more quickly than a conventional workplace:
* airborne hazardous substances can become more concentrated, and heat stressors can become more intense
* the space can fill with liquids or free flowing solids, and
* oxygen levels may become dangerously low
Working in confined spaces is a leading cause of death and injuries to many workers each year. An estimated 60% of the fatalities are among the attempted rescuers of a person in distress within a confined space. A confined space can be more hazardous than regular workspaces for many reasons.
In 2014, the Labour Program identified Part XI of the Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations - Confined Spaces, as a priority for review. The review identified the following issues:
* confusion in identifying various confined spaces and employer’s responsibilities towards those working in them
* certain safety provisions were outdated and did not align with industry practices and standards, and
* there was a lack of clarity in the regulatory text

* mitigate the risk of injury or death by improving the knowledge surrounding, and the identification of, confined spaces
* modernize and strengthen provisions and align them with industry practices and standards, and
* add clarity to promote compliance

seltz.title: Oxygen Deficient Atmosphere Hazards
seltz.snippet:
Oxygen deficiency is the result of an oxygen deficient atmosphere caused by leaking gases in confined spaces.

**While oxygen deficiency in humans is often the result of a medical condition, an oxygen deficient atmosphere in a confined space is just as dangerous**.

Except for drowning or being lost in space, most people don't worry about  a lack of oxygen. But if you are in a hospital, a restaurant, a bar or any of a hundred businesses or factories where they have stored tanks or cylinders of compressed gas nearby, than working or walking into an environment with a lack of suitable oxygen can occur. A leak in any of these tanks or cylinders in an enclosed area has the potential to lower the oxygen level, resulting in a hazardous oxygen deficient atmosphere.

## Understanding the Dangers of Oxygen Deficient Environments

OSHA defines an oxygen deficient atmosphere as anything less than 19.5% oxygen by volume. At lower levels, different physical symptoms can occur.

*Effects of Various Oxygen Levels*

|   |   |
| - | - |
|  Oxygen Level Percent | Effects |
|  20.8% | Normal - fresh air |
|  19.5-21% | Acceptable low oxygen (OSHA) |
|  10-19.5% | Increased breathing rate, accelerated heartbeat, impaired thinking and coordination |
|  6-10% | Nausea, vomiting, lethargy, leading to unconsciousness |
|  < 6% | Convulsions, cessation of breathing, cardiac arrest. |

See the Occupational Safety and Health Administration's (OSHA) 29 CFR 1910.134 standard and ANSI/ASSE Z88.2-2015 (Z88.2) guidelines for more information. seltz.title: Atmospheric Testing for Confined Spaces Training Guide | Train & Hire
seltz.snippet:
Your nose cannot protect you in a confined space. Some deadly gases have no odor at all, and hydrogen sulfide can knock out your sense of smell just as it reaches dangerous levels. The only way to know what is in the air is to test it with a working instrument, in the right order and in the right places. This is for people who test the air, including entry supervisors, attendants and experienced entrants. Reading it does not make you qualified. You need training on your own meter and your employer's procedures.

## What You Will Be Able to Do

- Explain the limits for oxygen, flammable gases and common toxic gases.
- Test a space in the right order, at the right levels.
- Bump test a meter, and say how that differs from calibration.
- Spot a reading that looks safe but is not.
- Set up ventilation that works, and retest it.
- Explain why inerted spaces need supplied air.

## What Counts as a Hazardous Atmosphere

OSHA's confined space rule treats the air as hazardous if any of these are true:

| Condition | Limit |
| --------- | ----- |
| Oxygen too low | Below 19.5 percent |
| Oxygen too high | Above 23.5 percent |
| Flammable gas or vapor | More than 10 percent of the lower explosive limit (LEL) |
| Combustible dust | At or above its lower explosive limit |
| Toxic substance | Above its legal exposure limit |
| Anything else | Immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) |

As a rough check for dust, OSHA notes that a cloud that hides objects 5 feet or more away may be at the limit.

## Oxygen

Normal air is about 20.9 percent oxygen. The levels below are approximate, and people react differently.

| Oxygen level | What can happen |
| ------------ | --------------- |
| 19.5 percent | Lowest acceptable level |
| Around 16 percent | Poor judgment and coordination, faster breathing |
| Around 10 to 12 percent | Blue lips, fainting |
| 6 percent or less | Collapse and death within minutes |

seltz.title: Oxygen-deficient atmospheres
seltz.snippet:
- Oxygen concentrations below 19.5 percent pose serious dangers to workers in confined spaces.

Normal air has an oxygen content of 20.8 percent. An atmosphere is considered oxygen-deficient when the available oxygen content is less than 19.5 percent. No atmosphere with less than 19.5 percent oxygen should be entered without an approved self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA).

When the oxygen level in a space drops below 17 percent, an entrant may experience rapid breathing and an accelerated heartbeat. As the oxygen content decreases further, additional physical effects arise, including poor muscle coordination, rapid fatigue, intermittent respiration, nausea, and an inability to perform tasks. At concentrations less than 6 percent, entrants rapidly lose consciousness and death occurs within minutes.

Oxygen deficiency occurs from chemical or biological reactions that displace or consume oxygen from the atmosphere in a space. Drivers of oxygen displacement and consumption include:

- The combustion of flammable substances, such as in welding, cutting, or brazing; and
- Bacterial action, such as in fermentation.

Oxygen deficiency due to bacterial action can occur in excavations and manholes located near garbage dumps, landfills, and swampy areas. Slow chemical reactions, such as in the formation of rust on the surfaces of metal tanks, vats, and ship holds, will also consume oxygen in the atmosphere of a confined space.

Most confined space deaths are caused by the air. Of the atmospheric hazards, the most basic is the wrong amount of oxygen. Too little oxygen can cause collapse in seconds and death in minutes, often with no warning at all. Too much oxygen turns ordinary materials into fuel and can make a small spark into a flash fire. This lesson explains how oxygen levels change in confined spaces, what happens to the body as oxygen falls, why enrichment is dangerous, and how to interpret an oxygen reading, including at altitude.

## Normal air

Normal air at sea level contains about 20.9 per cent oxygen by volume, about 78 per cent nitrogen, about 0.9 per cent argon and small amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases. The body does not respond to the percentage of oxygen directly. What matters is the partial pressure of oxygen: the share of the total air pressure contributed by oxygen. At sea level, where atmospheric pressure is about 101.3 kPa, the partial pressure of oxygen is about 0.209 × 101.3 ≈ 21.2 kPa.

you.title: Confined Spaces: Is 19.5 Percent Oxygen Really Safe? | EHS Today
you.snippet:
Some gases and vapors may be present at concentrations well above the TLV while, at the same time, they are below a combustible gas meter's limit of detection. Because ambient air contains about 20.8 percent oxygen, if the oxygen concentration in a space is anything other than 20.8 percent, you should ask yourself "Why?". If you can't come up with a credible answer, you had better not let people enter a space until you can do so. John Rekus is an independent safety consultant and author of the National Safety Council's Complete Confined Spaces Handbook.
Everybody knows that an oxygen level of 19.5 percent is safe for entry into confined spaces. Well, once again, what everybody knows is simply wrong!
For example, in the first case I worked on as an expert witness, the entry supervisor for a contract tank cleaning firm tested the atmosphere in a space and found it contained 20.1 percent oxygen. When I saw that number, I was concerned, very concerned. The supervisor wasn't; in fact, he was oblivious to the warning it provided. Instead, he testified with great confidence that he knew that 19.5 percent was "safe." After all, that's what he'd been taught at the confined space course he took at the state fire school.
The oxygen partial pressure inside a confined space may be lower than the 159 mm Hg found in ambient air. If so, the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveolar spaces also will be lower. If inert gases like argon and nitrogen enter a space, they displace some of the atmospheric air. When this happens, the amount of oxygen and, thus, its partial pressure goes down. For example, assume that nitrogen leaks into a space, lowering the oxygen level to 19.5 percent.
